lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 3 you met captions. What does a caption do? It tells you about a picture.
Texts that teach us facts are called information texts. They often have a title, headings, pictures and captions. Each paragraph has a main idea: the one big thing it is about.
The main idea is often in the first or the last sentence. The other sentences are details: facts and examples that support it.
Read this: Bees are busy helpers. They carry pollen from flower to flower, which helps plants make seeds. They also make honey. The main idea: bees are busy helpers.
A summary tells the main idea and the most important details in a few words of your own. It leaves out small details and your opinions.
Try it in the world: read a fact card in the game's Books, like the Planet Book. What is its main idea, and which details support it? Next: how texts are built.

exercises.prompt: Owls hunt at night. Their big eyes see in the dark, and their soft feathers let them fly without a sound. What is the main idea?
exercises.hint: What is the whole paragraph mostly about?
choices: Owls are made to hunt at night.
exercises.explain: Every sentence shows how owls are made for hunting at night.

exercises.prompt: Cacti can live in deserts. They store water in their thick stems, and their spines keep thirsty animals away. Which one is a detail?
exercises.hint: A detail supports the main idea. The main idea is the first sentence.
choices: Cacti store water in their stems.
exercises.explain: "Cacti can live in deserts" is the main idea; storing water in their stems is a detail that shows how.

exercises.prompt: The main idea is what a whole paragraph is mostly about.
exercises.hint: Think of the one big thing.
exercises.explain: Yes: the main idea is the one big thing the paragraph is about.

exercises.prompt: A detail is a fact or an example that supports the main idea.
exercises.hint: Details tell us more.
exercises.explain: Yes: details are the facts and examples that back up the main idea.

exercises.prompt: Where do you often find the main idea of a paragraph?
exercises.hint: Look at the start and the end.
choices: In the first or last sentence
In the middle of a word
exercises.explain: Writers often put the main idea in the first or the last sentence.

exercises.prompt: Beavers build dams. They cut trees with their strong teeth, pile up sticks and fill the gaps with mud. What does the text mostly tell us?
exercises.hint: Every sentence is about the same job.
exercises.explain: The text tells how beavers build dams, step by step.

exercises.prompt: Ants live in big groups. Some find food, some look after the young, and the queen lays eggs. Which is the best summary?
exercises.hint: A summary gives the main idea in a few words, without opinions.
choices: Ants live in groups where each ant has a job.
exercises.explain: Ants live in groups where each ant has a job: that covers the whole text. The others are one detail or an opinion.

exercises.prompt: A good summary includes your own opinion, like "I think it is great".
exercises.hint: Does a summary tell what the text says, or what you think?
exercises.explain: No: a summary tells what the text says, not your opinion.

exercises.prompt: Main idea: snow keeps some animals warm. Which detail supports it?
exercises.hint: Which one shows snow keeping an animal warm?
choices: Mice make tunnels under snow, out of the wind.
exercises.explain: Mice sheltering under the snow shows snow keeping animals warm.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps of writing a summary in order.
exercises.hint: You can't find the main idea before you read.
items: Write it in a few words of your own.
exercises.explain: Read, find the main idea, pick the key details, then write it in your own words.

exercises.prompt: Volcanoes can build new land. When lava cools, it turns to rock. Over many years, the rock piles up into islands. Which title fits best?
exercises.hint: A good title names the main idea.
exercises.explain: The text is about volcanoes building islands, so that is the best title.

exercises.prompt: Recycling saves materials: old cans become new cans, and paper becomes new paper. Which detail would ALSO support this?
exercises.hint: Which one shows an old thing becoming a new thing?
choices: Old glass can be melted into new glass.
exercises.explain: Old glass becoming new glass is another way recycling saves materials.

exercises.prompt: In this text the main idea is the last sentence: Frogs start as tadpoles. They grow legs and lose their tails. Frogs change a lot as they grow.
exercises.hint: Which sentence covers all the others?
exercises.explain: Yes: "Frogs change a lot as they grow" sums up the details before it.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence would NOT belong in a text about how penguins keep warm?
exercises.hint: Which one has nothing to do with staying warm?
choices: Penguins huddle together in the wind.
Thick fat keeps the cold out.
exercises.explain: Waddling is true, but it does not help penguins keep warm.

exercises.prompt: Details: fresh water every day, hay to eat, a clean hutch and room to hop. What is the main idea?
exercises.hint: What do all the details have in common?
choices: A rabbit needs care every day.
exercises.explain: All the details are ways to care for a rabbit.

exercises.prompt: Main idea: owls are made to hunt at night. Sort each sentence.
items: Their big eyes see in the dark.
Soft feathers let them fly quietly.
They hear mice moving under snow.
exercises.hint: Does the sentence show how owls hunt at night?
exercises.explain: Big eyes, quiet feathers and sharp hearing help owls hunt at night. Laying eggs and being brown are true, but they don't support that main idea.

exercises.prompt: Main idea: bees are busy helpers. Sort each sentence.
items: They carry pollen from flower to flower.
exercises.hint: A supporting detail shows bees helping or working. A true fact may still not show that.
exercises.explain: Carrying pollen, making honey and helping plants make seeds show bees as busy helpers. Their colours and their stings are true, but they do not show bees helping.

exercises.prompt: Put the beaver text in order: the main idea first, then its details.
items: They fill the gaps with mud.
They cut down trees with their teeth.
exercises.hint: Start with the main idea, then follow the steps the beavers take.
exercises.explain: The main idea comes first: beavers build dams. Then the details, in order: they cut trees with their teeth, pile up sticks, and fill the gaps with mud.

exercises.prompt: Match each text's details to its main idea.
exercises.hint: Ask what each set of details adds up to.
exercises.explain: Owls' eyes and feathers: made to hunt at night. Ants' jobs: they live in groups with jobs. Cacti's stems: they can live in deserts. Beavers' teeth, sticks and mud: they build dams.

exercises.prompt: Sort what goes in a summary of the bee text, and what to leave out.
items: They carry pollen, so plants make seeds.
One bee landed on my hat.
exercises.hint: A summary keeps the main idea and the big details; it leaves out opinions and tiny details.
exercises.explain: Keep the main idea and the big details: busy helpers, pollen for seeds, honey. Leave out opinions (I think bees are scary) and small details (one bee on a hat).
